Plaintiff appellant Haran Chandra Daradi who is the son of Shasi and the heirs of one of the original tenants, his sister Bhanu Sundari, plaintiff No. 2 and wife Brojabasi Dasi, plaintiff No. 3 together filed a suit for partition alleging that the suit land originally belonged to three tenants mainly Iswar Daradi, Kartik Daradi and Jagannath Daradi. According to the plaintiff these 3 persons were the original tenants. Iswar according to the plaintiff died leaving Feli Bewa, a childless widowed daughter and being a childless widow acquired no right of inheritance, but yet her brothers (cousins) namely Kudiram and Shasi Daradi (father of the present plaintiff) permitted Feli to possess the 4 annas 11 gondas 1 cara 2 krantis and 12 tils share in Khatian No. 444 and 929 and allowed her to posses 4 pies share in Khatian No. 764 just out of sympathy and not out of any right. The land was recorded in her name and she possessed the property accordingly. As to the other non-mentioning co-sharer namely Jadu Nath it is the plaintiff case that he had sub-let his land of the Khatian to tenant without, however, mentioning the name of those tenants. According to the plaintiff Feli Bewa had only 3.61 decimal of land in all those 3 Khatians but she transferred to Ananta Mondal and to a lady called Purna Bewa (her mother) an area totalling 6.10 acres out of those khatian whereafter Purna Bewa sold an area of .65 decimal of 'Gha' schedule property to defendant Nos. 6-11 and the rest to defendant Nos. 1 & 2. Plaintiff's further case is that Khokan, son of Khudiram, the heir of Kartik then sold from his share of .65 decimal to defendants 6-11 by registered kabala and sold the rest of his share to plaintiff No. 1 which was purchased in the name of his wife plaintiff No. 3 vide kabala dated 18th Chaitra 1365 B.S. It is the further case is that Baidyanath, brother of Khokan also sold from his share. 51 to defendant No. 5 and rest to one Saijuddin who in turn sold to plaintiff No. 2 sister of Haran, by a kabala dated 18th Chaitra, 1365 B.S. being Ext. 1 and Ext. A. Further case is that plaintiff No. 1 took settlement of rest of the land of Baidynath and Khokan, son of Khudiram and sold those to plaintiff No. 3 by kabala on the same date as stated already hereinbefore. Thus according to the plaintiff they are entitled to the share of 6.10 acres of land but their co-sharer are possessing in excess of their share. Hence the suit for partition. 

 8. In a partition suit the law is this that all who had interest of the same property, claiming under the same right need to be made a party and in their absence, the suit would not be maintainable. This is based on the principle of substantial justice and for the purpose of doing away with multiplicity of suits. The court of first instance would have jurisdiction to pass a decree in a suit when the suit was maintainable but passing a decree in 4 suit which was not maintainable, being barred by law, would be a decree passed without jurisdiction because the proceedings would in such a case be carom non judice. This is not a mere irregularity of procedure but an illegality which cannot be cured because of obvious prejudice caused to the non-impleading parties. 

 10. A case cannot be sent back on remand as matter of right. It is never sent back on remand as a matter of right for allowing the parties to change the nature and character of the suit or to correct mistake which initially had non suited the parties or for giving fresh evidence. 

 Under the law a defect in the plaint need be corrected at the earliest possible opportunity and any formal defect in a suit need be corrected immediately after it came to the knowledge of the party concerned but if a party chose to proceed with a suit in spite of the knowledge of the inherent defect in the suit, which would ultimately non suit him the party would be so proceeding and would be deemed to have proceeded with the suit with the knowledge of the legal consequence. Therefore, after long 15 years of filing of the suit in the court of first instance it would be an abuse of the process to allow the plaintiff to have the defect of parties corrected on remand which defect had been challenged by the defendant immediately in their written statement on 29.11.68, only 10 months after the suit was filed on 10.1.68. 

 Mr. Rahim has cited some other cases of Indian jurisdiction which have been quoted with approval in the case reported in 25 DLR wherein it was held that to allow to amend after long years would be to allow him to file fresh suit after long years of limitation allowing him to take advantage of his own negligence and default. It was further held in those cases that if a suit would have been totally non-maintainable because of improper pleading under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act or for that matter for not making the co-sharers a party in partition suit, if cured after long years at the second appellate stage, would mean making the suit maintainable with retrospective effect by passing the law of limitation, in cases where the suit will be barred under the Limitation Act. 

 14. Mr. Nizamuddin Haider has taken pains in expressing the ratio under reference by referring to the judgment of Teunon, J. in that case under report to the effect that a remand in such cases as to addition of parties may be made in case the trial had been vitiated by the court's erroneous decision on the preliminary question of non-joinder and because of the absence of the assistance which the added party was in a position to give. Reading the judgment as a whole it seemed that it was held by his Lordship that a trial be sent on remand to a de novo trial under Order XLI, rule 23, if the trial Court had disposed of the suit upon a preliminary point, and further held that the case would also be sent on remand when there was no proper trial because of the error caused by court in its procedural matters where, for example, a minor was termed as major or the trial has been vitiated by the Court's erroneous decision on a preliminary question of non-joinder.
